subject: Computer Networking
title: ARPANET's First Message
description: Learn ARPANET's First Message in one minute.

hook.text: On October 29, 1969, a student at UCLA typed 'LOGIN' to a computer at Stanford. The system crashed after 'LO'.

buildup.text: That two-letter transmission was the first message ever sent over ARPANET — the internet's ancestor.

discovery.text: ARPANET initially connected just four universities: UCLA, Stanford, UC Santa Barbara, and the University of Utah.

twist.text: The crash was a bug, not a design flaw. They fixed it and successfully logged in an hour later.

climax.text: From four nodes in 1969, ARPANET grew to dozens by the mid-1970s, connecting research labs across the country.

punchline.text: The internet's first word was 'LO.' Even legends have humble starts.

quiz.question: What was the first message sent over ARPANET?

details.summary: On October 29, 1969, the first ARPANET message was sent from UCLA to Stanford Research Institute. The word login was attempted, but the system crashed after the letters L and O. The network was quickly restored and the full message was sent, marking the birth of computer networking as we know it.
details.whyItMatters: ARPANET's first message was the beginning of the connected world. From two nodes in California, the network grew into the global internet connecting billions of people.
takeaways: The first ARPANET message was sent on October 29, 1969
The system crashed after two characters, then succeeded on retry
ARPANET connected four universities in its first year

faq.question: What were the first four nodes on ARPANET?
faq.answer: UCLA, Stanford Research Institute, UC Santa Barbara, and the University of Utah. Each had an Interface Message Processor connected to their mainframe. By December 1969, all four nodes were connected and communicating using the new packet-switching technology.

faq.question: How quickly did ARPANET grow after the first message?
faq.answer: ARPANET grew from 4 nodes in 1969 to 13 by 1971, 40 by 1973, and over 200 by 1981. Growth accelerated as universities saw the value of shared computing resources and electronic communication. By the mid-1970s, email had become the network's most popular application.
